headline: Gave notice to leave the 1992 UN climate treaty
how: Rejoin, likely with Senate consent.
why: The Senate ratified it in 1992, so under the rule used here re-entry needs Senate consent; the exit takes effect 2027-02-27, one year after notice.

headline: Pulled the US out of the World Health Organization
how: Rejoin, probably with Congress's approval.
why: CRS report R46575 reads the 1948 joint resolution as setting the terms of membership, so a pen alone is doubtful.

headline: Pulled the US out of the Paris climate agreement
how: Notify the UN. The US is back in 30 days.
why: The US joined Paris by executive agreement without a Senate vote, so the next president can rejoin with a pen.

headline: Quit UNESCO, the UN body for schools, science and heritage
how: Ask UNESCO to readmit the US, as in 2023.
why: The US has left and rejoined UNESCO by executive decision before, so a pen is enough.

headline: Pulled the US out of the UN Human Rights Council
how: Resume participation and run for a Council seat.
why: Participation is an executive choice with no Senate vote behind it.

headline: Cut off funding to UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees
how: Lift the funding ban in a 60-vote spending law.
why: Congress separately bars UNRWA funding in appropriations riders, so ending the order alone would not release money.

why: The Court ruled 6-3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that IEEPA, the emergency-powers law, does not authorize tariffs, so the order has no force.

why: It rests on Section 232 of the 1962 trade law, which lets the president set duties for national security, so no vote is needed.

headline: Charged steel, aluminum and copper duties on a product's full value
how: Revoke it. Charge on metal content only again.
why: It is a Section 232 national-security action, so the president can change it alone.

headline: Put a 50 percent tax on Canadian dairy, alcohol and vehicles

why: The 1930 statute lets the president impose duties up to 50 percent on countries that discriminate against US commerce, so a pen ends it.

headline: Stripped job protections from about 50,000 federal workers
how: Restore the protections with a new rule.
why: A final rule has the force of law and can only be replaced by another rule, which takes months of notice and comment.

why: The endangerment finding (EPA's formal finding that greenhouse gases endanger health) can only be reissued by a new rule, and the repeal is being fought in the D.C. Circuit.

how: Restore a cap with a new FCC order.

how: Rewrite the rules with new FCC orders.
why: A final rule has the force of law and can only be replaced by another rule, which takes months of notice and comment.

headline: Dropped the FTC ban on worker noncompete clauses
how: Start over with a fresh FTC rule.
why: The 2024 ban was struck by a court (Ryan v. FTC) and the FTC chose not to appeal, so restoring it means starting over.

headline: Canceled 83 percent of USAID's aid programs and ended their awards
how: Nothing. The money is gone; fund new programs.
why: Terminated awards and the lives and supply chains behind them cannot be restored, only replaced by new spending.

headline: Shut down USAID and folded what is left into State
how: Recreate USAID in law; needs 60 Senate votes.
why: USAID is written into statute, so only a new law can formally restore it, even though the State Department move was done by order.

headline: Handed Education Department programs to six other agencies
how: Cancel the agreements and bring programs back.
why: These are agreements between agencies, not laws, so the next president can end them; the Education Department itself still exists in statute.

headline: Cut about 317,000 federal workers through firings, layoffs and buyouts
how: Rehire. Nobody who left has to come back.
why: Hiring is an executive power, but the experience that walked out the door is gone, and about 154,000 left through the deferred resignation program.

headline: Mass-fired probationary workers; a court found OPM ordered it unlawfully
how: Rehire them through normal hiring.
why: Hiring is an executive power, but a court found OPM unlawfully ordered the firings and most people have moved on.

headline: Fired seventeen inspectors general by email on 2025-01-24
how: Replace them, with 30 days notice to Congress.
why: The judge found the firings likely broke the Inspector General Act but would not reinstate anyone, and the Senate has confirmed successors.

headline: Let presidents fire independent-agency heads at will (Trump v. Slaughter)
how: Nothing. Only a later Court or an amendment.
why: The 6-3 ruling overruled Humphrey's Executor (the 1935 case protecting independent commissioners), so any future president inherits the same power over FTC-style agencies.

headline: Federalized 2,000 National Guard troops for Los Angeles
how: Nothing. The troops left; do not reissue it.
why: The 2025-12-23 Supreme Court order read the statute's "regular forces" as the regular military, so a federalization order like this one is likely unlawful.

headline: Mobilized the D.C. National Guard with no end date

why: The president commands the District's Guard, so no court or Congress is needed; the Supreme Court's Trump v. Illinois order dealt with state Guards, not D.C.

headline: Created the Memphis Safe Task Force, with the Guard under the governor
how: Withdraw it and stand down the task force.
why: It directs federal agencies, which the president controls, and the Guard role rests with Tennessee's governor, so a pen is enough.

why: The 6-3 ruling holds universal injunctions likely exceed courts' power, so a 2029 president inherits the same limit on challenges to her own orders.

headline: Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs (Learning Resources v. Trump)
how: Leave it.
why: The 6-3 ruling struck the IEEPA tariffs. As precedent it also limits every later president's tariff tools, which a Democratic president can accept.

headline: Supreme Court struck down the birthright citizenship order (Trump v. Barbara)
how: Leave it.
why: The Court held the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to nearly all children born on US soil, so only a constitutional amendment could change it.

headline: Supreme Court kept the Guard out of Chicago (Trump v. Illinois)
how: Leave it.
why: The 6-3 interim order read "regular forces" as the regular military, which is a limit on every later president, though it is not a final ruling.
